<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with genuine clash. CON built a sharp, sustained dilemma (acceptance-gated links leave the first mover alone; ungated links bulk-export strangers) and a strong relational-ownership frame. PRO, however, controlled the weighing throughout: it established early that CON never contested the network-effect/exit failure, then answered the dilemma by leaning on "interoperable" as ongoing reachability (email/telephony), addressed the block/pseudonym pressure with a concrete opt-in, victim-side design, and in closing turned CON's own alternative ("bans on blocking exports," MySpace collapsing only when everyone fled) into evidence of the coordination problem and a portability-mandate-lite concession. CON's "compelled carriage" reply was a real cost but underdeveloped, and PRO's "structural failure vs speculative design flaw" comparison remained the cleanest decision rule. Minor ding to PRO for claiming CON "offered nothing" before CON's answer turn had occurred.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pointer/first-mover dilemma: CON's [A2.3]/[A3.1] pressure was sharp, but PRO's A1 in [B4.1]-[B4.3] reframed via interoperability (leaver stays reachable, reciprocity only where ties were already mutual, public follows unchanged), and PRO's closing then converted CON's own MySpace/"ban export-blocking" alternative into a concession of the coordination problem the motion targets.</best_rebuttal>
